newsitem.title: USA: Elvis Presley's manager Colonel Parker dies at 87.
newsitem.headline: Elvis Presley's manager Colonel Parker dies at 87.

text.p: "Colonel" Tom Parker, the manager who helped guide Elvis Presley's rise from young hopeful to King of Rock and Roll, died of a stroke on Tuesday, a friend said. He was 87.
Parker died at the Valley Hospital in Las Vegas a day after being admitted, said Bruce Banke, a close friend of Parker.

Parker, a carnival barker in his early years, managed Presley from 1955 until the singer's death in 1977, overseeing his rise to worldwide fame as a singer and movie star. Presley's fame has only grown since his death at the age of 42.
The "Colonel" before Parker's name was an honorary title.

"He was the world's greatest manager in my estimation. He took a boy singer from the streets of Memphis and made him into one of the world's greatest superstars," said Banke, retired publicist for the Las Vegas Hilton.
"He knew exactly how to market Elvis," said Banke, who got to know both Parker and Presley when the singer performed at the Las Vegas Hilton.
Banke said Parker was loyal and would not manage other stars. He and Presley were partners, he said. "It was more of a father-son relationship than star-manager," he added.
Presley's widow and daughter, Priscilla and Lisa Marie Presley, issued a joint statement saying they were "saddened to learn of the Colonel's death."

"Professionally and personally, he has been such a great and constant friend to us both ... He and Elvis were an amazing team and the work they did together changed the course of pop cultural history," they said.

Jack Soden, chief executive of Elvis Presley Enterprises Inc, the business empire left behind by the singer, said Parker's contribution to Presley's career was immeasurable. "He was a master promoter, a show business pioneer, a legendary figure in entertainment history," he said.

Movie star Ann-Margret, who starred with Presley in "Viva Las Vegas!", issued a statement saying she was sad at Parker's death. "He has been a part of my life since I was very young and from that time he had always shown me kindness and support," she said.
Parker told Variety in 1994 that he had had lots of offers to write books about Presley but had turned them all down. "You know what they want -- dirt," Parker said. "I'm not a dirt farmer."
Parker worked in carnivals before beginning to manage singers in the 1940s, eventually signing the young Presley.
Some accounts have portrayed Presley and Parker as having a stormy relationship and suggested that Parker managed the star's life with an iron fist.

A 1994 article in the San Diego Union-Tribune noted that Elvis purists viewed Parker as "the devil who traded the singer's rock 'n' roll soul for the demon Hollywood dollar." But it said Presley was quoted by a biographer as saying: "We more or less picked each other."

Dick Clark, executive producer of a television movie about Presley and Parker, told the Los Angeles Times in 1993 that, in the early years, Parker received 25 percent of Presley's income. In 1967, he increased his take to 50 percent, he said.

Little is known about Parker's early life. The 1993 edition of the Almanac of Famous People lists Parker as probably born in 1910 in Breda, the Netherlands, and lists a variant of his name as Andreas Cornelius Van Kuijk.
Parker, who lived in Las Vegas, leaves a widow, Loanne.
